entities.summary:
Willis Tower, formerly known as the Sears Tower, stands as an iconic skyscraper in Chicago, Illinois, completed in 1973. Designed by architect Bruce Graham and structural engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, it was the tallest building in the world upon its completion, reaching 1,450 feet (442 meters) including its antenna. Its construction, driven by the rapid expansion of corporate America, symbolizes the economic vitality of the 1970s and the architectural innovations that accompanied this growth. It has become a defining feature of the Chicago skyline and a pivotal point in discussions about urban development and architectural design in the modern era.

The Willis Tower's design incorporates a bundled tube system, which allowed for a taller and more stable structure, showcasing advanced engineering techniques of the time. The building's construction involved 2,000 workers over three years, with an estimated cost of $150 million. It originally served as the headquarters for Sears, Roebuck and Company, representing a significant shift in corporate architecture toward high-rise buildings that could accommodate thousands of employees in urban centers. The tower's observation deck has attracted millions of visitors, becoming a key tourist destination that enhances Chicago's economy.

The legacy of Willis Tower extends beyond its physical presence; it has influenced subsequent skyscraper designs worldwide, prompting a wave of vertical architecture that emphasizes both functionality and aesthetic appeal. Its status as a cultural landmark has been cemented through numerous representations in media and art, while it continues to inspire urban planners and architects. The building's transition from a corporate headquarters to a mixed-use space reflects broader economic trends, marking its relevance in the ever-evolving landscape of American urban life.
